issues.legal_issue: A rent court may use apportionment to fix standard rent when the premises were part of a larger demise, rather than let separately, on the statutory baseline date.
material_facts: The premises in dispute formed part of a larger estate let under a single tenancy on the baseline date.
The tenant later took a separate lease of the disputed premises and sought fixation of standard rent by apportioning the rent of the larger estate.
issues.conclusion: Apportionment is a permissible method of fixing standard rent in these circumstances when it is reasonably necessary and feasible to achieve a just result; it is not an inflexible rule.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5(8)(b), 5(10)(b), and 11(1), particularly section 11(1)(c), of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, read together, empower the court to fix a just standard rent where difficulty arises because premises were let at different times as a whole or in parts, or for another reason. The court should interpret the provisions consistently with the Act’s purpose of curbing extortionate rents and should not adopt a narrow construction that enables evasion of that purpose. Apportionment is a rule of justice and good sense, but must be applied with caution and in light of the circumstances. The court relied on Narayanlal Bansilal v. Venkatrao Anant Rai, Bainbridge v. Congdon, and Fox v. Bishop of Chester; it rejected the contrary approach in Dhanrajgirji Naraingirji v. W. G. Ward and did not accept Bata Shoe & Co. Ltd. v. Narayan Das Mullick as laying down a universal rule.

rule.if: standard_rent_fixation_case and premises_part_of_larger_demise_on_baseline and premises_not_separately_let_on_baseline and apportionment_feasible_and_just

predicates.standard_rent_fixation_case: A tenant or landlord brought a proceeding to determine the standard rent of premises.
predicates.premises_part_of_larger_demise_on_baseli: The premises were included in a larger property let as a whole on the relevant baseline date.
predicates.premises_not_separately_let_on_baseline: The premises whose standard rent was to be fixed were not let separately as a unit on the relevant baseline date.
predicates.apportionment_feasible_and_just: The circumstances made it reasonably feasible and just to allocate part of the larger property's rent to the premises.

issues.definition: When standard rent is being fixed for premises that were part of a larger letting on the baseline date, the court may use apportionment if doing so is feasible and just.

issues.legal_issue: Apportionment may be used for premises retaining their identity after the baseline date, while later construction and improvements may be assessed separately to provide a fair return on the landlord’s investment.
material_facts: The trial court after remand found that most of the disputed premises retained their identity, while several structures were new.
The reviewing courts fixed rent for the new structures by capitalising their value and allowed a return on the landlord’s investment.
For the old premises, the courts principally used apportionment and also allowed a return on the landlord’s investment in flooring, ceilings, and fixtures.
The premises had been parts of a larger entity comprised in a single lease on the baseline date.
issues.conclusion: The courts below applied apportionment properly to the unchanged premises and accounted for the new structures and relevant investments; their method did not warrant interference.
issues.legal_principle: Apportionment is not a rigid rule and must be adjusted to the circumstances. A court fixing standard rent should consider post-baseline investments and improvements, other relevant circumstances, and the physical advantages enjoyed by the tenant compared with the rest of the property. If the premises have completely changed their identity, apportionment may lose its efficacy and be abandoned. The Court applied the principles discussed in Bainbridge v. Congdon and upheld the factual findings concerning the identity of the premises and the treatment of the new structures.

rule.if: standard_rent_fixation_case and premises_part_of_larger_demise_on_baseline and existing_parts_retained_identity and new_structures_added_after_baseline and landlord_invested_in_improvements

predicates.standard_rent_fixation_case: A tenant or landlord brought a proceeding to determine the standard rent of premises.
predicates.premises_part_of_larger_demise_on_baseli: The premises were included in a larger property let as a whole on the relevant baseline date.
predicates.existing_parts_retained_identity: The court found that the existing parts of the premises had not completely changed their identity after the baseline date.
predicates.new_structures_added_after_baseline: New structures were built on the property after the baseline date.
predicates.landlord_invested_in_improvements: The landlord spent money on construction, repairs, or improvements to the property.

issues.definition: Where premises were part of a larger letting, their unchanged parts retain their identity, and later structures or improvements involved landlord investment, the court may apportion rent for the unchanged parts while allowing a fair return for the investment.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court should not interfere with factual rent-fixation findings that are not shown to be perverse or manifestly unjust.
material_facts: The lower courts found that most of the old premises retained their identity and used apportionment principally for those premises.
The lower courts assessed the land value associated with the new structures and fixed rent using their findings on the evidence.
The appellants challenged the factual findings and valuation, but the Supreme Court found no basis to regard them as perverse or manifestly unjust.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to re-investigate the factual findings and valuation, found no ground for intervention in its special jurisdiction, and dismissed the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: Whether premises changed identity after the baseline date is largely a question of fact. In an appeal by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court will not re-investigate factual conclusions that are not shown to be perverse or manifestly unjust. The Court also found no evidentiary basis for the asserted higher land value.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_against_rent_fixati: A party brought a special-leave appeal challenging a rent-fixation decision.
predicates.challenge_is_to_factual_findings: The appellant asked the reviewing court to reassess factual findings, including findings about the premises or their value.
predicates.findings_not_perverse_or_manifestly_unju: The factual conclusions were not shown to be perverse or manifestly unjust.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal concerning rent fixation, a reviewing court will not interfere with challenged factual findings when they are not perverse or manifestly unjust.
